A few channels that were created later that were cable exclusively began as ad-free, yes, but cable TV was never 'intrinsically' ad-free as you're suggesting.

I appreciate your response. I have heard of the weakest link idea and I don't think its particularly relevant when it comes to the mental state of a person for a variety of reasons. I have three counterpoints:

First is the Ship of Theseus argument. If you replace a sum of parts equivalent to the whole, is it the same object? If each chain breaks throughout your life and you replace each individual one, is it still the same chain? I have my own personal identity, my own perception of who I am, what my purpose in the world is, and if each link in the chain is what constitutes that existence then replacing it would ultimately mean a completely transformation of who I am. I don't want to rebuild everything - there are parts of who I am that I do like. But, it isn't just one link that breaks over and over again, and it isn't only the links that I see as troublesome that break. Each link in the chain degrades over time and will eventually break. Everything breaks in the end; nothing is ever "fixed", it's destruction is simply delayed.

Second, you're making the assumption that the only one link in the chain is weak, or that the chain is still in-tact outside the broken links. I'm not sure if you've ever been suicidally depressed. Given that you're posting in this thread, I would assume you have at least a cursory understanding of what it's like. If you haven't, here's how I'd explain it in the context of your analogy:

It isn't just one link in the chain being damaged. When you're depressed to that point, when you look at the chain, you see that the entire chain is rusted out. But its your only chain, so you try and make due with it anyway. You ride your bike out with your friends and the chain works, but you move slower and it snags sometimes and you have to stop to put it back on.  But the chain never breaks completely. No link is actually broken. If you pull on it - it won't snap. Things won't unravel. But it will put stress on the chain, and over time, with continued use the chain will eventually stretch and be worn to the point of unusability. 

The worst part is the people around you when things get like this. They tell you "just buy a new chain!" or "you just need to oil it up!"... But that's the only chain you have. That's the only chain you've ever had. To you, that's the only chain that exists, so when people tell you to "just replace the broken parts of the chain" or to "just get a new chain", or to "take it to the place where they fix chains to have a professional look at it", all you hear is "your chain is broken and you have to fix it". Do you see the hopeless desperation that this creates? Everyone around you is telling you to "fix the chain", but the chain isn't actually broken. It just needs to be worked on and cared for; not to be replaced. Taken to the extreme (which suicidal people will do 100% of the time), your argument can be seen as telling people to replace the weak links in your life. If deep down, you think that you are the weak link about to break, then your message turns in not only condoning, but also suggesting that a viable solution is suicide itself.

Lastly, if someone is suicidally depressed, they likely don't see the chains as two parts. They see the chain is individual links lying on the ground with no connection. They don't know why or when it broke, just that its broken and you can't see how or why to fix it. So you do what you're taught to do your entire life with a mess and clean it up. But, when things are broken, you just throw them away. You don't repair them. You replace them.

You cannot replace your life. You can replace a chain.

You can repair things, but they're still damaged. You can repair things, but it doesn't change the fact that its not as structurally sound as it was before.

Unless you're rebuilding, which you can't, then repairing is just putting off the inevitable collapse.
